The United Arab Emirates shut more beaches after an oil spill in the Persian Gulf raised concerns over environmental and health impacts.
Sharjah said Al Hamriya Beach has been closed as a precautionary measure to prevent pollution from the oil spill. Ras Al Khaimah said that all its beaches are closed until further notice, without specifying the reason for the closure.
On Friday the UAE’s climate ministry detected the spill off the coast Umm Al Quwain, north of Dubai, and temporarily closed all beaches and coastal areas in the emirate. It didn’t identify the tanker.
Odors in Umm Al Quwain, Sharjah and Ajman don’t pose health risks to residents, the ministry said in a post on X.
Specialized teams and relevant authorities were dispatched to Sharjah to undertake necessary measures to ensure the safety of beaches and prevent pollutants from reaching them, the emirate’s media office said.
The region has suffered oil spills and leaks in recent months. In August, a tanker ran aground near Oman’s southeastern coast leaving the country to battle a slick covering about six-and-a-half times the land area of Manhattan. Shortly after, Iran was dealing with an oil spill off Qeshm Island, near a breeding ground for endangered hawksbill sea turtles.
Conflict in the region is also increasing the risk of oil spills and maritime pollution.
A cargo vessel sank in the Strait of Hormuz this month after a strike that sparked a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said. Freighters struck by projectiles can leak ship fuel, even if the main oil storage tanks aren’t breached, endangering wildlife and marine environments.

Japanese companies are moving to pay compensation to users following waves of cyberattacks that have disrupted internet services and raised concerns about economic stability.
GMO Internet Group, a leading provider of online financial services, said customers would be compensated for losses stemming from unauthorized access following a cyberattack on its foreign exchange trading service, and all customers would receive 5,000 yen ($32) as a gesture of goodwill, CEO Masatoshi Kumagai said in a blog post on Sunday.
“The internet itself is now starting to break down,” said Kumagai, whose sprawling group includes internet infrastructure and cryptocurrency trading.
Shares of GMO, which had a market value of $2.6 billion as of Friday’s close, slumped almost 16% on Monday to a four-month low against a 0.2% rise in Tokyo’s benchmark index .TOPX.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the government planned to compile an emergency package of measures against cyberattacks by next week.
The government said on Friday it would set up a team to simulate cyberattacks using AI to identify weaknesses in technology systems as organizations scrambled to curtail risks from flaws in the PHP programming language that underpins much of the internet.
More broadly, Japanese companies are being roiled by attacks, with industry experts saying AI is helping automate tasks from scanning for software vulnerabilities to crafting phishing campaigns, making cybercrime faster, cheaper and harder to detect.
“The internet is increasingly being transformed into a tool that malicious actors use to threaten and rob people,” said Kumagai.
Government and company websites in Japan, Europe and elsewhere went offline last week after the disclosure of critical vulnerabilities in the PHP programming language prompted millions of hacking attempts.
Call on Japan to Step Up Cyberdefense
Kumagai has urged the Japanese government to apply defense measures in response to the cyberattack, after the introduction of a cyberdefence system this month.
The system could involve steps such as attacking hostile servers to neutralize threats.
“Now is the time for the public and private sectors to work together to protect Japan,” wrote Kumagai.
GMO said it received a demand for money from a party believed to be behind the attack, along with a threat to disclose company and customer information if it did not comply. In an update on Monday to his blog post, Kumagai said that the party had demanded $50 million in cryptocurrency.
GMO said it would not comply with the demand and would respond to the incident in coordination with police and other authorities. It did not mention any connection to PHP flaws.
The company, which will provide a free alternative service to its customers for six months, said it could not currently calculate the impact on earnings from the goodwill payments and compensation for losses.
White-hat hackers working for the company had identified security issues but the depth and speed of the response were insufficient, Kumagai wrote.

Assicurazioni Generali SpA plans to reduce around 9% of its workforce in Germany and downsize locations as part of a simplification effort in the European country.
Generali plans to set up five regional centers in Munich, Cologne, Karlsruhe, Hamburg and Saarbrücken, bringing together teams currently spread across Germany to reduce costs and strengthen collaboration, the Italian company said in a statement on Friday. The job reductions will mainly be achieved through “voluntary retirement arrangements.”
The insurer will invest “a three-digit million euro amount” in IT, digitization and artificial intelligence. It also plans to recruit new employees “with skills for the future.”
The planned job cuts are part of Generali’s broader push to streamline its operations and direct resources toward areas offering stronger growth and profitability. Under Chief Executive Officer Philippe Donnet’s strategy through 2027, Italy’s biggest insurer is seeking to accelerate growth in its preferred profit pools while simplifying its operating model, increasing automation and improving productivity.
In Germany, the company has already been cutting costs and modernizing its operations, with a target to reduce its cost-income ratio to 52% by 2027, from 57% in 2024. Generali had more than 9,000 employees in the country, where last year it generated over €15 billion ($16.8 billion) of premium income, according to its website.
The news was first reported by German outlet Manager Magazin.

General Manager Brian Horak walks down an aisle at Post 60 Market in Emerson, Nebraska. A new national report shows how everyday costs have increased for Americans (Kevin Hardy/Stateline).
Americans’ growing frustration over high prices has defined many political campaigns ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Rising costs of healthcare, gas and groceries during President Donald Trump’s second term have put Republicans on defense, not only in Washington, but in statehouse and gubernatorial races across the country.
As the political environment continues to sour for Republicans, a new analysis released by the Urban Institute on Monday underscores just how expensive everyday life has become in America: Gas and electricity prices are rising much faster than paychecks. Housing, childcare and healthcare are becoming a bigger strain for millions of people.
And affordability pressure is worsening in once-affordable havens such as Atlanta; Louisville, Kentucky; and Rochester, New York, where costs of housing, groceries and healthcare are increasing faster than the national average.
The latest installment of The American Affordability Tracker from the left-leaning think tank details how costs of food, housing, energy and healthcare have changed across all 50 states over recent years. High prices are pinching people across income brackets, with an estimated 49% of families unable to afford the basic costs of living. That’s according to Urban Institute’s true cost of economic security calculation, which measures how much is needed to live securely.
“We’re not saying that 49% of people are poor. We’re saying that they’re not secure,” said Gregory Acs, an Urban Institute fellow who worked on the research project. “Even if they’re paying all their bills, they’re paying all their bills at best.”
He said the analysis confirms that the economic angst so many people feel is justified — despite strong national economic indicators such as low unemployment and growing gross domestic product.
“They are not crazy. They’re not making it up,” Acs said. “They’re not being marketed into feeling bad. They really do have struggles.”
Among other findings, the report shows that average annual childcare costs for two young children have risen $6,600 over the past decade. Since January 2025, gas prices have risen by 33% — an average increase of $1.02 per gallon nationally. And premiums for benchmark plans on the Affordable Care Act Marketplace are up 22% since last year, now averaging $611 per month.
Affordability politics
Those struggles have become a political liability for Republicans, who control the White House, both chambers of Congress, most state legislatures and a majority of governor’s offices.
All midterm elections, as a referendum on the sitting president, are difficult for incumbents in the majority. But this cycle is particularly charged because of Trump’s promises to improve the economy during his 2024 campaign, said Todd Belt, a professor of political management at The George Washington University.
“He hasn’t done that. In fact, in a lot of ways, he’s made things worse,” Belt said, citing Trump’s unilateral war in Iran and tariff policies — both of which have driven up costs. “And so Donald Trump is bringing down the Republican ticket.”

Investing.com -- Goldman Sachs expects the Federal Reserve to hold rates at this week's meeting but deliver a second hike in December, stating in a note Monday that FOMC participants appear to have settled on a compromise of raising rates at every other meeting.
Economist David Mericle said the Fed's hawkish pivot has tightened broad financial conditions moderately since September.
However, he noted that the tightening is only slightly more than is usually associated with one rate hike, and much less than the four hikes the market had priced. As a result, the FOMC is unlikely to view it as excessive or as a replacement for hikes.
Goldman said a key question is how the Fed will modify the statement language referring to its September hike. The bank thinks it may adapt language from a recent speech by Vice Chair Philip Jefferson.
"We do not expect significant new information from the press conference," Mericle wrote.
He added that seemingly strong support for hiking every other meeting sets a high bar for deviating from that plan through year-end.
If the Fed maintains that pace in 2027, "it could consider hiking in March," said Mericle. However, he does not expect that outcome.
"We do not expect a hike in March because we expect the inflation trend to improve as the effects of tariffs, the energy shock, and AI price pressures diminish," the economist said.
However, Goldman said a March hike is possible if inflation data come in worse than expected.
"The most important risk is that oil futures are above our forecasts, largely reflecting concerns about potential further conflict with Iran," Mericle said.
Market pricing now peaks just above 4.5%. Goldman's forecasts are considerably less hawkish, as the bank is skeptical the Fed will hike four times and expects "cuts down the road."

Can Exxon’s $4.5 Billion Refining Windfall Defy Dropping Crude Prices on Oct. 30?
Exxon's refining business delivered a historic quarter, but crude prices moved sharply against it heading into the Oct. 30 earnings call. Find out which force came out on top and what it means for the stock's remarkable 13% run.
Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM | XOM Price Prediction) reports third-quarter results on Oct. 30. A projected $4.5 billion refining boost runs into lower average crude prices, and this report will show which force carried the quarter.
Refining Muscle Powered a Huge Second Quarter
Last quarter, Exxon earned $14.5 billion and generated $23.6 billion in operating cash flow while temporarily losing roughly 10% of upstream production to Middle East disruptions. Free cash flow exceeded $17 billion, and net debt fell by more than $7 billion.
Refining did the heavy lifting. About 3 million barrels a day of industry capacity sat idle because of the Strait closure, and CEO Darren Woods said on the July call that Exxon expects “a very robust refining market with very high margins.” Gulf Coast reliability exceeded 95%, and diesel output set a second-quarter record.
Shares have gained 13.63% over the past month, closing at $183.21 on Oct. 23.
Wall Street Expects Earnings to More Than Double
The quarterly EPS consensus has rose from $3.2767 90 days ago.
Refining Gains Versus Crude and Derivative Drag
The net math is what matters. Energy Products should collect roughly $4.5 billion in added earnings, but lower average Brent prices could create a $1.3 billion upstream drag. An estimated $2.5 billion paper loss from derivative timing effects adds noise. Those timing effects cost $3.88 billion in the first quarter, so you should focus on underlying earnings.
Upstream volume is the second test. Guyana reached about 900,000 barrels per day and the Permian exceeded 1.8 million oil equivalent barrels per day last quarter. I want an update on the Errea Wittu FPSO, which management targeted for start-up by year-end, and on the Golden Pass LNG ramp.
Capital returns matter too. Exxon plans $20 billion in 2026 buybacks and has extended dividend growth to 43 consecutive years, the kind of run that puts it firmly in the Dividend Kings club we ranked by valuation in a free report. Structural cost savings reached $16.3 billion against a $20 billion target for 2030.
Finally, listen for management’s tone on windfall taxes. Rising refining profits have renewed scrutiny in Washington, and Exxon runs 850,000 barrels a day of capacity in the U.K. and Europe, where similar levies are under discussion.
A Real Test of Exxon’s Through-Cycle Pitch
Management has argued that Exxon can perform across market cycles. This quarter tests that claim directly, because refining, upstream growth and cost cuts must offset lower crude and complex derivative accounting. If underlying earnings hold up and buybacks stay on pace, the stock’s run has a stronger foundation. Keep an eye on fourth-quarter refining commentary, since that will shape whether the windfall lasts.

More companies have been turning to open-source models from US and Chinese AI developers, which are less expensive and can be run locally or on private clouds.
Frontier developers Anthropic and OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) have responded to demand for more affordable models.

PG vs. CL: Which Household Giant Deserves Your Retirement Dollars?
Both Procter and Gamble and Colgate-Palmolive just raised their dividends and beat earnings estimates, but one of them has a balance sheet vulnerability and a troubled turnaround that retirement investors cannot afford to ignore.
Procter & Gamble (NYSE:PG | PG Price Prediction) or Colgate-Palmolive (NYSE:CL): which one better fits an investor seeking income for retirement? Both just raised their dividends. Both keep beating estimates: P&G posted its 6th straight beat and Colgate its 5th straight beat. The checks they mail to shareholders still differ by a wide margin, and so do the reasons to own each one.
Yield and Income: P&G Pays the Bigger Check
P&G raised its quarterly dividend to $1.0885 from $1.0568. The increase amounts to roughly 3%. Colgate moved to $0.53 from $0.52, a raise of about 1.9%. P&G also yields more, at 2.61% against Colgate’s 2.15%.
Colgate covers its payout with more room to spare. Its 2025 dividends of $1.82 billion took about 50% of free cash flow. P&G’s fiscal 2026 dividends of $10.23 billion used about 68% of roughly $15.1 billion in free cash flow. That ratio still leaves P&G enough cash to plan more than $10B in dividends and ~$5B in buybacks for fiscal 2027. Colgate’s balance sheet has less buffer: shareholders’ equity stood at just $236M after years of buybacks.
Winner: P&G. It pays the higher yield, raised faster, and covers the payout well.
Growth Trajectory: Colgate Is Gaining Speed
Colgate raised its 2026 outlook at its last earnings report, and now guides for mid-single-digit Base Business EPS growth. Gross margin expanded 140bp to 61.5%, and Base Business EPS of $0.99 exceeded the $0.95 estimate.
P&G’s quarter was strong too: core EPS of $2.00 beat the $1.89 estimate, and organic sales rose 4%. Still, management held core EPS guidance at 0% to 3% growth because of a ~$1.4B after-tax commodity hit. Management put it this way: “The strength is real, but it won’t be a straight line.”
Investors are paying for Colgate’s faster growth. The stock rose 22.77% over the past year, while P&G gained 9.59%. Both now trade near 21 times forward earnings. Colgate’s main weak spot is North America, where organic sales fell 3.0%. Its CEO said “it won’t be a linear improvement” but promised sequential increases.
Winner: Colgate. Its guidance is rising while P&G’s stays flat.
Long-Term Track Record: P&G’s 136-Year Record Stands Alone
P&G has raised its dividend for 70 consecutive years and paid one for 136. Colgate’s streak of increases runs 63 consecutive years. TIPS or Dividend Stocks? How Retirees Can Keep Up With Inflation
Two very different tools promise to shield retirement income from rising prices, but each carries a trap the other avoids. Knowing which trap you can live with changes the answer entirely.
On October 23, 2026, the 5-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Security (TIPS) carried a real yield of 2.34%, and the 10-year TIPS carried 2.66%. On the same day, the ordinary 10-year Treasury yielded 5%. A real yield is the yield a bond pays on top of inflation. If you buy a TIPS and hold it to maturity, you lock in that yield above whatever the Consumer Price Index records. Meanwhile, the research inflation index for Americans 62 and older rose 3.6% through September 2026, and Social Security’s 2027 cost-of-living adjustment is also 3.6%. This edition sets TIPS against Procter & Gamble (NYSE:PG | PG Price Prediction), one of the market’s longest-running dividend growers.
How TIPS Work and What You Get Back at Maturity
The Treasury sells TIPS in 5-, 10-, or 30-year terms. With most bonds, the principal remains fixed. A TIPS principal rises with inflation and falls with deflation, adjusted using a version of the Consumer Price Index published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (TreasuryDirect).
The interest rate, determined at auction, never falls below 0.125%. The Treasury pays that rate every six months on the adjusted principal. The rate remains fixed, but the dollar amount of each payment changes as the principal moves with prices. Purchases start at $100. The Treasury issues new 5-year TIPS in April and October, and new 10-year TIPS in January and July. You can also buy issued TIPS through a brokerage at market prices.
At maturity, you get back either the inflation-adjusted principal or the original principal, whichever is larger (TreasuryDirect). That floor has limits. It protects the original face value, which isn’t always the price you paid. A buyer who pays more than face value on the open market, or who purchases a bond that has already built up inflation adjustments, can get back less than they paid if deflation follows.
Three more limits apply. First, the real yield you get depends on when you buy. The market real yield changes every trading day, so the 2.66% from late October is a snapshot, and it is locked only for buyers who hold to maturity. Second, if you sell early, the price can fall: when real yields rise, existing TIPS lose value, so selling before maturity can mean a loss.
Third, reinvestment risk: interest payments and maturing principal get reinvested at whatever real yields exist at that point, which could be much lower than today’s. U.S. government support guarantees both the stated coupon and the return of principal. That support doesn’t protect the market price before maturity, nor can it make the CPI match your budget. The senior-focused index puts extra weight on housing and medical care, and no benefit or bond is tied directly to it.

Dave Obelkevich’s first experience with the New York City Marathon was in 1973, when it had fewer than 400 entrants and took place entirely in Central Park. He was on the west side of Manhattan near 100th Street when a pack of runners in bibs flew by. He asked a few onlookers what was going on. “It’s the marathon,” they said.
A recreational runner himself, he was both impressed and intimidated by the lead runners’ speed. He knew he couldn’t keep up with them for 26.2 miles, but he figured he could probably finish one of the four loops of the park at a respectable pace. So, on their final lap, he jumped in and finished in 43 minutes. After that, he immediately signed up for the following year.
Obelkevich admits that it took a couple of years for his training to gel. In the months leading up to the 1974 race, he did just one six-mile training run a week. “I took six days off,” he says, laughing. He still managed to finish in 4:20:27, but the experience itself was “tough,” he says.
The now 83-year-old registered again in 1975, but didn’t finish the race. He’d started strong but suffered a series of dizzy spells. With five miles to go, he’d stopped to take a break when the late Fred Lebow, race director and cofounder of the New York City Marathon, drove by. Discouraged by the time he’d lost, Obelkevich asked Lebow for a ride to the finish line. “He should have said, ‘Hell no, you finish by walking!’ But instead, he said, ‘Yeah, get in the back.’ So it’s his fault I didn’t finish,” Obelkevich says, jokingly.
In 1976, the marathon course changed to include all five boroughs of New York City. “It ran through much of the city I’d never seen,” Obelkevich says. He grew up in a suburb of Binghamton, New York, and moved to Manhattan in 1961 to attend Columbia University, but he’d always lived on the Upper West Side. “I don’t think I’d ever been to Staten Island. It was an eye-opener,” he says.
By the time he reached the start line of that first five-borough marathon, Obelkevich was, thankfully, running more than six miles a week. He’d joined the Millrose Athletic Association, where he’d picked up some solid training habits and gained a whole new social circle.
He’d discovered that, in a group of runners who shared similar goals and challenges, he was more extroverted than usual. “I opened my mouth and spoke to a complete stranger. It’s not that hard to do. It’s just a matter of getting started. So that changed my whole personality,” he says. That year, he finished the marathon in 3:22:44.
From that point on, Obelkevich has never missed a New York City Marathon, making him the runner with the longest streak on record: 49 races. This November, he’ll share a 50th anniversary with the course as it’s known today.

I’m going to say something obvious: Racing can be very hard and uncomfortable. An obvious result of this is people are often tempted to stop running.
So if you’ve ever been in the midst of a competition—on a hot day, on a tough hill, at the course’s halfway point—and thought of dropping out, it’s not just you. As solitary as those moments can feel, they are happening to athletes all around you, too.
Elite runners aren’t immune, either. Conner Mantz said that he entertains the thought in every race, and he’s an American record holder! Author and coach Steve Magness shared in a Twitter thread that the feeling is very common among pro runners. Morgan Beadlescomb confirmed he has—and has overcome—these thoughts all of the time.
So these two things can be true—many runners consider stopping and many of them complete races every year. It’s possible to successfully navigate these thoughts.
I’ll give you an example of how I navigated a moment like this that turned into one of the best races of my life.
It was pretty early in the 2022 New Bedford Half Marathon, and I had dug myself into a hole. The race started at 11 a.m. on one of the first warm spring days of the year. I went out way too fast, with a 5:06 first mile, followed by a series of tough uphill climbs. By the third mile, as I was climbing a big hill in the sun, my brain was deep into doubtful thoughts. There’s no way I can keep doing this. I messed up. Maybe today isn’t my day.
Instead of stopping, I started a negotiation—with myself. I wasn’t near the start line, and I knew it was going to be a long walk home if I stopped where I was. I made an offer, to myself, that I would drop out when I got closer to the starting area, around mile 4.
Once I reached mile 4, I was a bit more relaxed and still in one piece, so the pitch became How about we drop out at mile 7 and we jog back toward the start? Once I got to the 7-mile mark, the effort was hard, but not overwhelming. So when the course reached a 3-mile loop, I bargained again, with the option to drop out at mile 10. When I hit the 10-mile mark, it occurred to me that I had actually PR’ed in the 10-mile distance and that I would likely run a decent time even if I slowed down to a jog, so the bargain was that I could back off on effort instead of stopping.
I reached a big hill at mile 12, and the next deal was that I could stop after I got to the top of the hill. But when I got to the top, there was maybe a minute or so of running remaining, and I went in for a massive kick. I finished in 1:08:59, a PB by 32 seconds, in a race where I once had been convinced that I was going to drop out at mile 4.
Looking back, I used two mental tools. Life coaches call them “bargaining” and “chunking.”
The series of negotiations put me in a position to think about the race as a collection of smaller distances within it, or “chunks.” In my head, I was no longer running a 13.1-mile race. Instead, I was racing for a few miles at a time. This allowed me to panic less and focus a little more, moment to moment. It helped me to calm down and eventually find my stride. The physical sensations were the same, but committing to race just a few more miles was easier to wrap my head around. I could focus a little more.

Management put that figure at 11% of fiscal 2026 core earnings per share, compared to 8% in its July outlook.
That is a real cost, though it appears smaller when measured against the cash P&G brings in. Cash is the third. Operating income covered interest expense 22.0 times over the last twelve months. JPMorgan Chase's (JPM +0.74%) asset management division recently released the 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions report, an annual research report that includes 10- to 15-year return projections. For the first time, it has a returns forecast for Bitcoin (BTC +0.32%), and expects the top cryptocurrency to outperform the major asset classes.
It's another sign of the growing acceptance of cryptocurrency. CEO Jamie Dimon previously called Bitcoin a fraud, and as recently as 2025, he said he didn't see its value. However, a positive forecast doesn't necessarily mean Bitcoin is a slam-dunk investment.
What JPMorgan projected
JPMorgan's base case for Bitcoin is 10% annualized returns over the next 10 to 15 years, but the bank sees a wide range of potential returns. Its bear case is -11.2%, and its bull case is about 16.5%.
For perspective, JPMorgan forecasts annualized returns of 7.5% for U.S. large-cap stocks, 7.7% for small-cap stocks, 5.5% for gold, and 5.6% to 6.6% for U.S. bonds. Real estate investment trusts (REITs) came in at 8.2%.
If JPMorgan's base cases are accurate, $100 invested in Bitcoin would grow to $259 over the next 10 years. The same amount invested in large caps would grow to $206.
This isn't a buy recommendation from JPMorgan
The press release for JPMorgan's report specifically noted that Bitcoin isn't included as an allocation. The bank also hasn't yet included Bitcoin in its main covariance matrices, the models it uses to determine how much of an asset belongs in a portfolio.
JPMorgan laid out two obstacles to Bitcoin portfolio use: volatility and unstable correlations with other assets. Cryptocurrency is known for its volatility, and in Bitcoin's case, JPMorgan assumes 55% annualized volatility, compared to 18% for U.S. large caps and 17.2% for gold.

This includes how fast Google Cloud grew, whether Search held up, and what the capital spending number looks like. But one line matters more than any of them right now, and it sits a few pages deeper in the release: operating cash flow.
In the second quarter, Alphabet spent $44.9 billion on property and equipment and generated $39.1 billion in cash from operations. Before Florida lawmakers in 2022 enacted sweeping insurance law changes that cut the legs out of what had been called an excessive and burgeoning number of property claims lawsuits, they tinkered for years with ways to rein in the costly litigation.
One of the statutes, approved in 2021, required policyholders to give insurers 10 days’ notice before filing lawsuits. That law, the result of Senate Bill 76, was seen as a way to give carriers a second chance to settle a claim before litigation erupted.

Five Florida appeals courts have offered opinions on the retroactivity of Statute 627.70152, most of them differing in one way or another.
In 2023, the state’s 6th District Court of Appeal sided with the homeowner in a case known as Universal Property & Casualty Insurance vs. Rebecca Hughes. The judges found that the 2021 law did not apply retroactively and that the homeowner was not required to give pre-suit notice—even though Hughes’ suit was filed a month after the law took effect.
The 6th District’s opinion conflicted directly with the 4th District Court of Appeals, which had held in 2023 that the presuit notice requirement applies retroactively—to policies in effect at the time the law took effect. The 6th District asked the Supreme Court to settle the matter.

“So, on its face, no provision of section 627.70152 speaks to application of the statute to insurance policies issued before the statute’s effective date. And nothing in our precedent demands that we disturb that silence,” the opinion reads. “The correct answer is to respect the Legislature’s choice not to clearly require retroactive application of the statute.”

Utah’s lower legal blood alcohol concentration limit for drivers was associated with reduction in alcohol-related crashes over four years, according to a new study from the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety.
For the four years after the state lowered the limit to 0.05% Utah saw a nearly 9% reduction in alcohol-related crashes, according to an IIHS study.
Utah became the first state to lower its BAC threshold for impaired driving from 0.08% to 0.05% in 2018. It remains the only state with the lower limit.
IIHS researchers analyzed crash data from the first four years after the change and compared Utah’s alcohol-involved crash rates with those in Arizona, Colorado and Idaho.
Relative to the years before the law took effect, the share of Utah crashes involving alcohol fell further after implementation of the 0.05% limit. The percentage of injury crashes involving alcohol declined 12%, according to the study.
The share of crashes involving alcohol in Utah fell 12% to 21%, while alcohol-involvement rates increased in the comparison states, compared with Arizona, Colorado and Idaho, the study shows.
Researchers also accounted for the COVID-19 pandemic, which was accompanied by an increase in alcohol use and impaired driving nationwide. Alcohol-involved crashes in Utah rose 46% from March through May 2020, but the increase was short-lived. Over the 34-month pandemic period studied, the average monthly share of crashes involving alcohol increased 6%.
According to IIHS researchers, Utah presents some challenges for comparison because the state historically has had one of the nation’s lowest rates of alcohol-involved crashes. The law also received substantial publicity more than a year before it took effect, which researchers say may have influenced driver behavior before implementation.
The 0.08% limit became universal in 2005 after the federal government tied certain highway funding to adoption of that standard.
The National Transportation Safety Board recommended in 2013 that states lower BAC limits to 0.05%, citing impairment in depth perception and reaction time at that level.

The Archdiocese of New York and attorneys for about 1,300 parishioners who said they were sexually abused by clergy have agreed to an $800 million settlement of their legal claims, the second-largest involving a Catholic archdiocese in the U.S.
Archbishop Ronald Hicks sent an email Saturday to clergy confirming the settlement after attorneys for the survivors of alleged abuse announced it. Hicks said the agreement will not be final until the parties sign it, an action scheduled for the week of Nov. 6.
The only larger settlement over sexual abuse claims in the U.S. was by the Archdiocese of Los Angeles, which agreed in 2024 to pay $880 million to 1,000 abuse victims, in addition to $740 million in claims it had paid previously. In June, the Archdiocese of San Francisco agreed to a $395 million settlement over about 500 lawsuits filed over clergy abuse, and in December 2025, a federal judge approved a settlement in which the Archdiocese of New Orleans agreed to pay at least $230 million to abuse victims.
The agreement with the New York archdiocese would end more than seven years of lawsuits. The parties agreed to a framework for an agreement in May that required everyone who filed a claim to sign off.
“The unanimous agreement of survivors who filed claims against the Archdiocese of New York marks a powerful moment in the pursuit of justice,” Jeff Anderson, an attorney representing people who filed more than 1,000 of claims against the Catholic Church in New York state, said in a statement. “Through their courage, sacrifice, and determination, survivors have helped bring about a reckoning and a meaningful step toward accountability.”
The Archiocese of New York covers the city’s boroughs of the Bronx, Manhattan and Staten Island as well as seven counties to the north of New York City and is home to about 300 churches, more than 150 parochial schools and 2.5 million Catholics.
In his email to clergy, Hicks said that if church members ask about the settlement, “please let them know that much progress has been made.”
“We are on the verge of being able to, please God, bring some measure of healing and reconciliation to all victim-survivors,” he wrote. “This agreement will also allow the archdiocese to turn its full attention once again to its mission of preaching the Gospel, healing the sick, caring for the poor and needy, welcoming the stranger, and educating our children.”
A New York law enacted in 2019 allows survivors of child sexual abuse to file lawsuits against their abusers and institutions that shielded them until they turn 55. People who had already had turned 55 when the law was enacted also were given until August 2021 to file lawsuits, no matter when the alleged abuse occurred.
“This is an extraordinary achievement for the survivors,” said Trusha Goffe, an attorney in Anderson’s firm. “The survivors remined resolute through years of litigation to reach this monumental settlement.”

Federal regulators crack down on organ donation groups
The Organ Transplant Service teams at Walter Reed National Military Medical Center started using robotic surgery for kidney transplants in 2018. Nationwide, more than 109,000 people are on waiting lists for organ procurement. (Photo courtesy of Walter Reed National Military Medical Center)
Federal regulators are cracking down on the nonprofits responsible for coordinating organ donations, aiming to begin shutting down substandard groups by early next year.
New criteria will score the organizations on donation and transplantation rates and will decertify the bottom tier, meaning their contracts with the federal government will be revoked. Many professional medical groups welcome more stringent evaluations. But the nonprofits strongly oppose aspects of the criteria and have filed lawsuits, warning of potential disruptions in some states or regions.
More than 109,000 people are on waiting lists nationwide for organ procurement, according to federal data as of July. The majority of patients await kidneys. Each day on average, about a dozen patients die waiting for an organ.
State- and region-based nonprofits known as organ procurement organizations recover organs from deceased donors and work with families and transplant centers to coordinate donations. The procurement organizations have faced heavy scrutiny in recent years, with media reports and research papers highlighting issues such as skipping over some transplant centers and sicker patients, which worsens racial and socioeconomic disparities in organ transplants.
The feds have shut down at least two groups in the past two years, citing questionable practices and saying that there were cases in which workers ignored signs of consciousness in donors.
Changes have been in the works for years. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services first announced the new evaluation framework in 2020, in response to an executive order from President Donald Trump. Earlier this year, CMS released proposed revisions to that rule.
Aiming for better accountability, transparency and oversight of the groups, as well as increasing patient protections and organ recovery, CMS will score the nation’s 55 organ procurement organizations based on their donation and transplantation rates.
It will rank them into three tiers: Top tier organizations — those calculated in the top 25% of organizations for donation and transplantation rates — would be automatically renewed for another four years. Those that fall in the second tier will have the opportunity to improve and reapply for certification, while those ranking in the bottom tier would be decertified entirely. Other nonprofits will then make bids to the federal government to take over their service areas, according to CMS.
The new evaluation method has stirred debate. Some medical and policy experts say better oversight of the nonprofits is long overdue, while organ procurement organizations say they will face logistical hurdles in coordinating lifesaving organs if some are shut down.
CMS hasn’t yet released which organization’s contracts will be renewed or dropped, but said in March that the process would begin sometime late this year. The current four-year contracts expire in January, but CMS has said it will issue extensions as needed to ensure organ transplants continue.
CMS did not provide a specific date in response to Stateline’s request for information about when it would release certification

Want to end redistricting wars? Start by uncapping the US House.
The U.S. Capitol on April 9 (Ashley Murray/States Newsroom).
Missouri’s congressional redistricting battle has taken voters on a dizzying tour of the court system leading up to the midterms. After trips to the Missouri Supreme Court and federal district court resulted in different rulings, the state took not one but two trips to the U.S. Supreme Court, which held – twice – that the state should use its 2022 congressional map for the November 2026 election. Voters will decide the fate of the new map through Proposition A.
The legal question that dominated these disputes was about whether Missouri could use a newly drawn map despite a valid referendum petition. But the process invokes a larger and more important question about our representation: why has control of a single congressional seat become so consequential that politicians are willing to fight over it in multiple court rooms instead of trusting voters to decide?
One way voters can take matters into their own hands is to support uncapping the U.S. House of Representatives. From our nation’s founding until the passage of the Permanent Apportionment Act of 1929, the House grew alongside the national population. The cap at 435 members created an artificial scarcityaround representation, and that scarcity is one of the drivers fueling the current gerrymandering wars, in Missouri and beyond.
With the same number of House seats representing a population that has more than tripled since 1929, each individual district has become larger, and political control of each one has become more consequential.
Missouri’s congressional delegation provides a particularly striking example. When the House was capped in 1929, Missouri had 16 seats in the House, representing a population of 3.6 million residents, or approximately 225,000 constituents per representative. By contrast, today Missouri has only eight House seats, representing a population of nearly 6.3 million, meaning that each representative has approximately 783,000 constituents. In other words, Missouri’s population has nearly doubled yet its House delegation has been cut in half.
The average Missourian now experiences a much lower quality of representation as a result, because even the most conscientious representatives struggle to serve such large districts. For example, Missouri’s 6thCongressional District, spanning all of northern Missouri from the Kansas border to the Mississippi River, includes 39 counties and is so large that it covers more square miles than nine U.S. states.
To be clear, uncapping the House is not a panacea for partisan gerrymandering. The process will always be political, and the parties will always compete to control the process. But expanding the House would reduce the artificial scarcity problem that has made each individual seat such an extraordinarily valuable political asset. More representation is also consistent with what the Founders intended – in Federalist No. 55, Madison warned against making the House too small, arguing that it must be large enough to secure “a full knowledge of the interest of its constituents,” and ensure “that its members are not lifted too far aloft from the mass of the citizens.”
Smaller districts would also mean more opportunities for voters to elect someone responsive to their communities and less political power concentrated in each individual seat.

Only 29% of older parents said the same. Among the adult children, 49% believed inheritance conversations have the potential to trigger family conflict—which is one reason so many people avoid having them.
My book, Unspeakable, came out the same day as the survey, and that data provided an illustration of the book's core idea in the book: Many families are avoiding conversations because they're afraid of discomfort, even if this avoidance can cause harm. Estate planning is just one of the topics I cover in Unspeakable, but as I've traveled to give talks and answer questions about the book, it's one that's coming up most frequently.
In my work advising family businesses, I see this avoidance in various forms. In many cases, older parents hire my firm to help them inform their children about their estate plans. This is complicated work, but I find it fulfilling because I believe that in most cases, relationships become better when financial secrets are brought out into the open.

Born and raised in Latin America, Jose was educated as an accountant and worked for investment banks before founding a wildly successful private equity firm. The couple, who now live in San Francisco and are in their eighties, have built substantial wealth. Their assets total over $1 billion.
They have four children in their fifties, all well-educated and financially independent. Years ago the parents gave each child a significant gift—about $25 million each. IBM’s Software Business Sped Back Up
The turn came in software, which generated 44.4% of IBM’s revenue in fiscal 2025, more than any other segment. Management said software revenue growth jumped four points from the second quarter to reach 9%. It also said the division led a broader pickup across IBM’s segments, with infrastructure growth rising to 5%.
Management said the biggest difference came from a single part of the software business. On the October 21 call, executives explained that transactional sales, the software IBM sells in individual deals rather than as recurring revenue, make up about 20% of the software book. These sales fell by double digits in the second quarter, taking 4 to 5 points off software growth. In the third quarter, they rose by double digits. This swing was larger than software’s four-point pickup. Management also said its automation business faced a tougher comparison.

Management said about a quarter of the jump came from large deals that slipped out of the second quarter and closed in the third. The other three-quarters was new business. For transaction processing, its mainframe software, management said the deferred second-quarter deals landed on top of a normal third-quarter mainframe buying cycle.

It's the first time the report has put a range on Bitcoin's returns, and it comes with a handful of heavy caveats. Although the figures it calculated are unlikely to prove true in 2036, the drivers for those results are hard to argue against, and it's my view that JPMorgan Chase is directionally correct. Here's why.
JPMorgan Chase's base case expects a lot of volatility
The JPMorgan Chase report is largely about the investing implications of the macroeconomic conditions facing the world during the coming years, touching on everything from inflation to global warming and, of course, Bitcoin.
It expects artificial-intelligence-driven productivity gains to push the U.S. economy's real growth rate to 2.1% annually, with inflation averaging 2.4% in the same period. It also raised its expected annual return for large companies, such as those in the S&P 500 index, from 6.7% to 7.5%, citing strong profit margins.
But it contends that Bitcoin will be buoyed by three different factors that will offer better performance than this.
The most important driver, with a 65% weight in the calculation, is Bitcoin's slowing supply growth relative to global money growth. The second-most-important factor, with a weight of 30%, is Bitcoin's inclusion in portfolios alongside allocations to other scarce store-of-value assets, such as gold. The last driver is the weakest: the coin's increasing network activity.

To gauge whether Adobe (ADBE) stock can jump 50%, look at a part of the company you may overlook: its faster-growing subscriptions for business professionals and consumers. In seven of the last ten calendar years, the stock rose 50% or more from one close to a later close in the same year. Yet the shares lost 27.0% over the past year, and you probably still think of Adobe as software for creative professionals. So how big are those subscriptions?
Business Professionals And Consumers Bring Adobe 29% Of Subscriptions
Adobe sold $1.91 billion of subscriptions to business professionals and consumers in fiscal Q3 2026, up 16% from a year earlier. That pace makes them the faster-growing group so far. Adobe’s subscriptions for creative and marketing professionals were far larger at $4.65 billion, but grew 13%.
Adobe maintains a wide reach with business professionals and consumers. On the September 10, 2026 call, management said monthly active users in this group rose more than 25% from a year earlier to over 900 million. The company is also targeting the next generation of business professionals by making student spaces in Acrobat available globally.
Adobe Is Choosing When To Turn Users Into Subscribers
Adobe says it will decide when to try to turn free users into paying subscribers. Management said on the September 10 call that the company is routing part of its traffic to its freemium products, which are free to start, to win customers and deepen their usage. Adobe will then convert those users into recurring revenue at the right time. This strategy, management added, balances winning new customers with growing recurring revenue.
Analysts questioned that approach on the call. When one analyst noted that net new annual recurring revenue was down 36% to 37% from a year earlier, management cited the shift toward freemium products as one of the drivers. Adobe finished fiscal Q3 2026 with $22.16 billion in remaining performance obligations, which represent contracted revenue the company has yet to book. That figure was up 8% from a year earlier.
Trading at 14.0 times Adobe’s last twelve months of earnings, against 22.9 for the S&P 500, the stock price appears to allow for little from those users. Adobe’s faster-growing business and consumer subscriptions show reported sales are still rising, but they do not settle the analysts’ questions about new recurring revenue. Management raised its fiscal 2026 revenue and earnings targets on the call, but it only reiterated its target of 10.2% growth in ending annual recurring revenue.
What Adobe Passed Up To Win New Users
Adobe opted not to focus on pricing actions in its creative business so it could keep adding users. Management said on the September 10 call that the company was glad it had held back. Pricing actions might have brought short-term relief, management said, but they mattered less than winning new users.
The creative business still makes up most of Adobe. For fiscal 2026, management targets $18.242 billion to $18.272 billion of subscription revenue from creative and marketing professionals, against $7.47 billion to $7.49 billion from business professionals and consumers. If more of Adobe’s new users do not start paying, the company will have skipped pricing actions in its largest business without the new subscribers to show for it.

Tropical Cyclone Arnab is expected to hit India’s east coast on Wednesday, marking a break in an otherwise calm season that’s been subdued by a severe El Niño.
Arnab is currently 859 kilometers (534 miles) southwest of Kolkata, packing top sustained winds of 213 kilometers per hour, according to the US Joint Typhoon Warning Center, equivalent to a Category 4 hurricane. The cyclone is forecast to intensify further before making landfall, though models are currently split on whether it will stall before or after crossing the coast, the center said.
El Niño has upended typical cyclone seasons around the world this year. The Atlantic Ocean is set for one of its lowest hurricane counts since 1941, while the Northwest Pacific Ocean is on track for one of its most intense typhoon seasons on record. Meanwhile, the North Indian Ocean has seen significantly below-average activity in recent months, with Arnab the first cyclonic storm.
“One of the key climatic events has been the suppression of the Indian monsoon and with it, the much reduced tropical cyclone activity, driven by the long reach of the El Niño,” said Christian Werner, managing director of Global Weather Climate Analytics.
Arnab is expected to bring moderate to intense rainfall across parts of Andhra Pradesh and Odisha, and could cause widespread damage to standing crops and plantations including banana, papaya, and drumstick trees, according to the India Meteorological Department. Deluges over Nepal, Bangladesh, and Sri Lanka are also possible, forecasts show.
The North Indian Ocean sees storm activity peak during two distinct periods of the year: before the monsoon, from April to June, and after the monsoon, from October to December.

Voters line up outside Shiloh Hills Baptist Church in Kennesaw, Georgia, on Election Day, May 19, 2026. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)
The U.S. Department of Justice plans to send election monitors to every state ahead of Election Day, expanding a longstanding practice that’s spurred concern this year among Democrats and voting rights advocates because of President Donald Trump’s push to influence elections.
The Justice Department for decades has deployed monitors across the country to watch the voting process. During President Joe Biden’s administration, the DOJ sent monitors to 64 jurisdictions across 24 states for the 2022 midterm elections.
The 2026 monitoring program is larger, with the Justice Department announcing it will have a presence in all 50 states. DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels told States Newsroom on Monday that about 1,000 monitors will be involved but that the department won’t disclose the full list of monitored locations until Election Day — Nov. 3.
“Every monitor will merely observe and report any potential violations of federal law to the Department, which will be reviewed after Election Day,” Pels said in a statement.
Lawsuits prompt unease
While election monitors, who watch polling places and election officials for compliance with federal voting rights laws, have long been a feature of U.S. elections, the Trump administration’s extraordinary moves to assert federal authority over state-run elections have left many Democrats and even some Republicans uneasy about this year’s expansive effort.
The Justice Department has sued dozens of states in an attempt to force election officials to turn over voter lists that contain sensitive personal data, such as driver’s license and Social Security numbers. The DOJ has lost 27 cases so far, and won none.
Less than two weeks ago, the Justice Department sued California to block election officials from counting ballots from roughly 20,000 voters it says are suspected noncitizens.
And on Friday, the DOJ sued Alaska to preemptively prevent the certification of its U.S. Senate election if the Republican incumbent loses by less than the number of votes received by another candidate of the same name, citing the potential for voter confusion.
But concerns about DOJ monitors began building in August after Wyoming Gov. Mark Gordon, a Republican, expressed reservations about monitors, calling their actions “very odd” after DOJ personnel watched voting in the state’s primary election.
Andrew Walchuk, senior policy director and counsel for voting & fair representation at the watchdog group Common Cause, told reporters last month that monitors in and of themselves are nothing new, pointing to the long history of the DOJ’s monitoring program.
“But with this administration, we will be watching their activity very closely,” Walchuk said.

The percentage of people without health insurance is growing
Dr. Navdeep Lehga sets up equipment in the exam room of a mobile clinic in Mendota, California in 2025. The percentage of working-age adults without health insurance has grown in the past two years, according to a new report. (Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local)
The percentage of working-age adults without health insurance has increased in the past two years, largely because many people can no longer afford Obamacare coverage after Congress allowed federal subsidies to expire at the end of last year.
The uninsured rate for adults ages 19-64 rose to 11.2% this year, up from 8.9% in 2024, according to a new analysis by the Commonwealth Fund, a health policy and philanthropic nonprofit.
Nearly half of the 7,362 working-age adults who participated in the group’s biennial health insurance survey said they were uninsured, underinsured, or experienced a gap in coverage this year. Half said they delayed or avoided getting medical care because of the cost, compared with 46% in 2022.
The subsidies significantly lowered the cost of Obamacare coverage — making it free or nearly free for some people with low incomes. But the aid was designed as a temporary pandemic-era measure, and Congress allowed it to expire at the end of last year.
As a result, the percentage of working-age adults with health insurance from the marketplaces created under Obamacare, officially known as the Affordable Care Act, declined to 6% this year, from 8% in 2024.
The percentage of working-age adults enrolled in Medicaid also declined, to 13% this year from 16% in 2022, as many states removed people from the rolls at the conclusion of the COVID-19 pandemic.
The increase in the uninsured rate almost certainly will accelerate in January, when the Republican tax and spending law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act takes effect. That law will require many Medicaid recipients to prove they are working or engaging in approved community service activities for at least 80 hours a month.
The law also mandates that states verify enrollees’ Medicaid eligibility every six months.
Another factor in the growing percentage of people without coverage is the rising cost of healthcare, which is pushing up premiums for private insurance.
“It’s affecting people’s ability to pay off bills right away, and it’s having an effect on health plans,” said Sara Collins, a senior scholar at the Commonwealth Fund and the lead author of the report.
Almost a third of the survey respondents, whether insured and uninsured, said they currently had medical or dental bills or were paying off medical debt. And more than 70% of uninsured adults said they had cost-related problems getting care.
“I think it’s very concerning,” Collins said. “We know from our survey data that not going to get care isn’t and just generally is not good for people’s health over the long run.”
The rise in the uninsured rate comes after a long period of progress: Between 2010 and 2025, the overall uninsured rate in the United States fell by half, to 8% from nearly 16%, largely because of the Affordable Care Act.

The Western District Court of Appeals found that a man resentenced in 2023 must receive credit for time served on all four concurrent sentences
Deandre Pointer, serving four concurrent 23-year-sentences in the Missouri Department of Corrections, won a ruling Tuesday that he must get credit for all time he has served on all four counts of his conviction. If he had lost, Pointer would have been incarcerated for 40 years. He is shown in a 2025 interview (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
A Missouri man who should have been eligible for release in 2024 remains in prison because the state miscalculated his credit for time he had already served, the Missouri Western District Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday.
Deandre Pointer was sentenced to 23 years in the Department of Corrections on four counts, two of second-degree murder and two of armed criminal action, with the sentences to run concurrently. He received the sentence in 2023 after a Jackson County judge determined Pointer was abandoned by his public defender in a post-conviction case filed after his original sentence was handed down in 2005.
When the resentencing was finished, Pointer thought he would be out in about a year, when he had served the required 85% of the sentence. But when a Missouri Department of Corrections record clerk finished processing his paperwork, his projected release date was 2044.
The department misapplied the law on how to calculate his sentence, Judge Alok Ahuja wrote in the court’s unanimous opinion.
“The Missouri Supreme Court has held that, ‘in construing (state law), we are guided by the principle that criminal statutes must be ‘construed strictly against the (s)tate and liberally in favor of the defendant,’” Ahuja wrote.
The 2023 resentencing changed both the charge in one count, from first- to second-degree murder, and the way the sentences were imposed, from consecutive to concurrent.
“Pointer’s conviction and sentence for first-degree murder on Count 1 must be treated as if they never occurred,” Ahuja wrote.
In a 2025 interview with The Independent, Pointer said he pursued a new sentence because he was a victim of crime, forced to help the perpetrator out of fear for his own safety.
The stress of having to fight for release after winning his resentencing has taken a severe toll, he said at the time.

“I never took anxiety meds,” Pointer said. “Never in my life. Now, you know, I have to take anxiety meds just to have a functional day.”

The Western District decision overturned a February ruling from Cole County Circuit Judge Brian Stumpe that found the department had calculated the sentence correctly.

Mark Kiptoo has had some pretty memorable trips to Frankfurt. He won the city's marathon in 2014, returned four years later to set a then-world record for runners over 40, and on Sunday added another achievement to the list. This time, at 50 years old.
The Kenyan distance runner finished the Frankfurt Marathon on October 25 in 2:15:24, averaging roughly 5:10 per mile across 26.2 miles. He placed 13th overall, but his performance was particularly impressive for another reason: It was the fastest marathon ever recorded by a man in the 50–54 age group—and it wasn't especially close.
For 35 years, the M50 record belonged to South Africa's Titus Mamabolo, who ran 2:19:29 in Durban in July 1991. Kiptoo cut four minutes and five seconds off that mark on Sunday, a substantial improvement that now awaits official ratification by World Masters Athletics.
Kiptoo has barely had time to get used to being 50. He celebrated his birthday on June 21, less than two months after finishing 2:12:21 at the Geneva Marathon. That performance came too early to qualify for an M50 record, but it offered a pretty good preview of what he could do once he entered the age group.
Frankfurt wasn't even his first record-setting performance this month. On October 4, Kiptoo won the San Sebastián Half Marathon in Spain in 1:03:57, establishing a new M50 world-best time for the distance. Three weeks later, he was back on a starting line, this time with twice as many miles to cover.
Kiptoo didn't start competing until he was 28, entering his first race in 2004 while serving in the Kenyan Air Force. He went on to win the African 5,000-meter title in 2012, but didn't make his marathon debut until age 37. That first 26.2 was in Frankfurt, where he finished second in 2013, just one second behind the winner.
He also lost roughly a year of training to Achilles tendon trouble and the pandemic, according to the Frankfurt organizers. He returned to win the Zurich Marathon three years in a row from 2023 through 2025, clocking 2:09:16 in his last victory at age 48.
Before Sunday's race, Kiptoo told organizers he hoped his running would inspire people not to give up or stop taking care of their bodies as they got older. Running a 2:15 marathon at 50 certainly gives him a pretty persuasive example to point to.

State regulators just forced two major brokerages to pay back millions in commissions their customers never knew they were losing. The same quiet erosion could be happening inside your 401(k) right now.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Small stock trades aren’t always cheap ones. On Oct. 15, state securities regulators announced a $4.4 million settlement involving two Wells Fargo (NYSE: WFC | WFC Price Prediction) brokerage units and Merrill Lynch, part of Bank of America (NYSE: BAC). The North American Securities Administrators Association (NASAA) said the firms had charged unreasonable commissions on thousands of small-dollar stock trades.
What Regulators Found on 256,000 Small Trades
Massachusetts regulators led a multistate investigation that uncovered unreasonable commissions on more than 256,000 stock trades over five years. The problem was minimum commissions, which can turn even a modest transaction into an expensive one.
The two Wells Fargo units collected nearly $3.9 million in unreasonable commissions across approximately 228,243 trades between Sept. 30, 2020, and Oct. 1, 2025. Merrill Lynch accounted for another $549,000 in excessive charges during the same period.
Affected customers in participating states will receive refunds plus interest, and the firms must certify that they’ve changed their commission practices. The investigation concerned retail brokerage accounts, not specifically 401(k)s. But workplace retirement investors can face trading commissions through brokerage windows, along with fund expenses and other charges that quietly eat into their savings.
A $250,000 Balance and a Fee Nobody Noticed
Picture a hypothetical 55-year-old with $250,000 in his 401(k). He never sees a separate bill for investment expenses, so he assumes his plan costs him nothing. But his funds and plan charges run an extra 0.5 percentage point a year compared with similar, lower-cost options.
On his current balance, that difference amounts to roughly $1,250 in one year, assuming the balance doesn’t change.
Now stretch the comparison over a decade. Suppose the cheaper portfolio earns 6% annually after fees, while the more expensive one earns 5.5%. With no additional contributions, his $250,000 would grow to approximately $447,700 in the cheaper option, compared with $427,000 in the pricier one.
That’s a difference of nearly $20,700 from an additional half-percentage-point in annual costs, compounded over 10 years.
Four Places 401(k) Costs Hide
- Fund expense ratios. These expenses are built into the fund’s returns rather than billed separately on your statement. You can find them in your plan’s investment disclosures and fund documents, but it’s easy to overlook their effect on your balance.
- Administrative and recordkeeping fees. These pay for running the plan: recordkeeping, legal work and the website. Some plans charge a flat dollar amount and others take a percentage of assets. When they come out of your account, they show up on your statements.
- Managed account or advice fees. A 2025 NEPC survey found that 46% of participating retirement plan sponsors offered managed accounts. These services may charge an additional asset-based fee on top of the expenses of the underlying investments.

Cisco Is Up 47%, IBM Is Down 13%. Which Dividend Stock Is Better for Retirement?
Cisco and IBM have moved in opposite directions this year, and that gap reshapes which one actually puts more money in a retiree's pocket over time. The answer depends on which trade-off you can afford to make.
Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO | CSCO Price Prediction) or IBM (NYSE:IBM): which old-guard tech dividend holds up better for someone saving for retirement right now? This year, the two stocks have gone in opposite directions. Cisco is up 46.77% year to date at $111.03. IBM is down 13.13% at $252.18. That gap changes how much income a new buyer gets today.
We compared the two on three things that matter to anyone living off dividends: current income, payout safety and the balance sheet, and the business growth that pays for future raises.
Current Income: IBM Writes the Bigger Check
IBM yields 2.67%, compared with 1.56% for Cisco. Its forward annualized dividend is $6.76 per share. Cisco’s is $1.68. IBM has paid consecutive quarterly dividends every year since 1916, and its April 2026 raise was its 31st consecutive annual increase. Cisco’s run stands at 15 consecutive years.
IBM’s weak spot is how slowly the payout grows. Its quarterly dividend went from $1.66 in early 2024 to $1.69, a gain of about 1.8%. Over the same period, Cisco’s rose from $0.39 to $0.42, about 7.7%. Still, for retired people spending income now, IBM pays far more per dollar invested. Winner: IBM.
Payout Safety and Balance Sheet: Cisco Has More Cushion
Cisco paid $6.6 billion in dividends in fiscal 2026 out of $14.18 billion in operating cash flow, so the dividend used about 47% of operating cash. Its forward dividend works out to roughly 33% of the low end of fiscal 2027 non-GAAP EPS guidance, which is $5.05 to $5.11. Cisco closed the fiscal year with $15.9 billion in cash and investments. It also has $8.1 billion left on its buyback authorization.
IBM’s coverage is tighter. Over nine months, it paid $4.8 billion in dividends against about $8 billion of free cash flow, or 60%. Its forward dividend is about 58% of trailing EPS of $11.72. Debt stood at $63.8 billion, including $12.7 billion tied to its financing arm, against $11.1 billion in cash. That follows $11.4 billion in acquisitions this year. CFO Jim Kavanaugh described “a solid investment-grade balance sheet,” and he’s right, but Cisco has more room for error. Winner: Cisco.
Business Momentum: Cisco’s AI Networking Cycle Pulls Ahead
Cisco’s fiscal fourth-quarter revenue rose 17.6% to $17.25 billion. Non-GAAP EPS of $1.22 beat the $1.17 estimate, its fifth straight beat. Product orders rose 35%, and AI infrastructure orders reached $9.3 billion for the year. Chief Executive Chuck Robbins said, “We believe we are only at the beginning of this super cycle.” The weak spot is gross margin, which fell to 66.3% from 68.4% as AI hardware made up more of sales.
IBM’s third-quarter revenue grew 4.7% to $17.10 billion, with Red Hat up 11%. Consulting grew just 0.2%, and IBM Z revenue fell 20%. Full-year guidance calls for 4% to 5% constant-currency growth. That rate supports small, steady raises and little more. Cisco’s valuation premium is modest: 20 times forward earnings versus 17 for IBM. Winner: Cisco.

In brief
- Intel, Oracle, IBM and IonQ joined the list of companies objecting to trading of their shares on OKXICE TSV, according to its Oct. 26 notice.
- The total has climbed from nine on Oct. 15 to 26, though the notices don’t explain the objections or their effect.
- The notice says it’s uncertain whether tokenized shares in self-custodied wallets would be protected by SIPC if the tokenizer’s broker-dealer failed.
The tech sector’s resistance to tokenized stocks keeps building.
Intel, Oracle, IBM, and quantum computing firm IonQ are the latest companies to object to having their shares traded on OKXICE TSV, according to an updated public notice from the venue dated Monday.
The planned platform, a 50-50 joint venture between NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange and OKX’s U.S. holding company, now lists 26 objecting issuers.
That’s up from 22 in its Oct. 23 notice, which added Wells Fargo, Cisco, and Marvell. The tally stood at 16 on Oct. 19 and nine on Oct. 15, when the first batch included Verizon, Broadcom and UnitedHealth Group. In less than two weeks, the list has nearly tripled.
Technology companies dominate the roster. Microsoft, Alphabet, Broadcom, Qualcomm, Arm, Cisco, and now Intel and Oracle have all objected, along with banks Goldman Sachs and Wells Fargo.
IBM and IonQ add two quantum computing players. As before, the notices don’t explain the companies’ reasons or what an objection means for whether a stock can trade on the platform.
OKXICE TSV plans to let approved users trade tokenized U.S. stocks 24/7 through permissioned Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on OKX’s XLayer blockchain, paired with stablecoins such as USDC.
Users must pass identity and sanctions checks and hold a nontransferable “soulbound” token to trade. The venue is set to operate under the SEC’s innovation exemption, which the agency unveiled in September after the Clarity Act stalled in the Senate.
The latest notice highlights a key risk for investors. Each token represents a claim on a real share held by a third-party “tokenizer” through a registered broker-dealer. If that broker-dealer failed, the notice says, it’s uncertain whether tokenized shares in a self-custodied wallet would count as customer property or be covered by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation, which protects brokerage customers when firms fail.
The notice also says trades must be fully funded, with no margin or borrowing. Liquidity providers don’t have to be registered market makers and can pull their liquidity at any time.
OKX and ICE first teamed up on tokenized securities earlier this year before unveiling plans for the venue this month.

Procter & Gamble (PG) kept its forecast for fiscal 2027 earnings unchanged on October 22, 2026, even as management raised its estimate of the extra costs the company faces over that year. Management said the outlook includes higher raw material, energy, and transportation costs, and that its cost estimate assumes Brent crude oil at $100 a barrel. You will want to know how high those costs are against P&G’s earnings, since it is not settled yet whether the forecast can hold.
How Big Is P&G’s Cost Hit For Fiscal 2027?
Management now puts the combined fiscal 2027 hit from input costs, currency, and other items at about 11% of fiscal 2026 core earnings per share, its adjusted measure. This is up from 8% on the July call. P&G still forecasts core earnings per share growth of 0% to 3% for the year, so the company has to make up the whole hit elsewhere to land in that range. During the fiscal Q1 2027 call on October 22, 2026, analysts asked about the raised cost outlook and how P&G would respond to higher oil prices.
P&G’s reported gross margin fell to 49.8% in fiscal Q1 2027, down from 51.4% in fiscal Q1 2026. Management has said commodity and freight costs, along with spending to build demand, offset its productivity gains in the quarter.
How Does P&G Plan To Cover The Higher Costs?
Management has said P&G will cover the costs with savings and with price increases that come with new products. The company delivered about $500 million to $550 million of productivity savings before tax in fiscal Q1 2027, and management expects those savings to be heavier in the second half of the year.
So far, P&G has raised prices only a little. The company drew 0.4 points of its sales growth in fiscal Q1 2027 from higher prices, against 2.4 points from higher volume. Management will not say how much more P&G will charge, beyond saying that it prices with innovation and that new products are usually timed with retailers’ shelf resets.
Management has not said where in its forecast range earnings will land. It is confident P&G will finish inside its range, but said that after one quarter, the company needs time to work out where. Management has also said large further rises in commodity costs are not built into that range.
P&G Expects Even Higher Costs In Fiscal Q2 2027
Management has said cost headwinds will be materially higher in fiscal Q2 2027, which ends in December, because oil prices have stayed high for longer. It also said everything it knows is already built into its outlook. P&G is expected to report that quarter in January 2027, and its reported gross margin for the period, measured against the same quarter of fiscal 2026, is the figure to watch.

Banks that keep outside AI agents out of customer accounts are guarding their own revenue rather than their customers, Bianco Research president Jim Bianco said on Unchained’s Bits + Bips during a live stream on Oct. 26.
“Are you protecting me, or are you protecting your own profits?” he asked.
His example was JPMorgan Chase, which keeps third-party AI agents from signing in to Chase accounts or acting on them for customers. Jamie Dimon, the bank’s CEO, explained the policy to analysts on Oct. 13, warning of “rogue agents” and saying JPMorgan is “not going to allow just any outside agent to come inside the company” because that is “too risky for clients and for JPMorgan.” A spokesperson told Fortune that “protecting our customers is our top priority,” adding, “We support secure, customer-authorized data sharing through open banking providers.”
Citi, Bank of America and Wells Fargo have taken steps to limit third-party agents as well, and Charles Schwab CEO Rick Wurster has said the brokerage is shutting out third-party agents that try to move funds in customer accounts. Wells Fargo’s revised online access agreement, which takes effect Nov. 24, says transactions by an AI agent a customer authorizes are treated as the customer’s own, and makes the customer responsible for the agent’s unintended actions until the customer tells the bank it has revoked the agent’s access.
Get Unchained’s crypto news in your inbox with the free Unchained Daily newsletter.
A Model Built on Friction
Bianco said the traditional finance “business model is based on laziness.” Customers don’t want to log in every day to move idle cash into a money market fund, he said, but an agent could do it for them. In his account, banks profit by investing deposits that pay the customer nothing. “Now that you’re able to do it, the banks are afraid they’re gonna lose that revenue stream,” he said.
He put the money sitting in “zero-yielding bank accounts” at $4 trillion. Noninterest-bearing deposits in the domestic offices of U.S. banks came to about $4.04 trillion at the end of June, roughly 21% of domestic deposits, according to the FDIC’s Quarterly Banking Profile. That category includes business operating accounts, not only household savings. JPMorgan Chase Bank held $628.8 billion of it, about 28% of its domestic deposits, according to FDIC BankFind data.
Bianco made the same case about credit cards, saying issuers want cardholders to pay annual fees without making full use of their points, while some users have turned to AI agents to maximize rewards.
Pushback From Customers
Bianco predicted that customers would press for access anyway, noting that people already trade away their privacy online. “I think the public is gonna start demanding more and more of this,” he said.
Co-host Ram Ahluwalia, founder and CEO of Lumida Wealth Management, agreed on the motive. “They’re protecting themselves,” he said on the stream, adding that “the agents here are acting as fiduciaries of the customer.” He cautioned against overstating the risk of agent-driven deposit flight, though, since frictions such as opening a new bank account remain.

Third quarter earnings season is in full swing this week, with corporate results on deck from Big Tech heavy-hitters Microsoft (MSFT), Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), and Amazon (AMZN).
Aside from Big Tech, industries from oil to chips to pharmaceuticals will be represented, as Exxon Mobil (XOM), Intel (INTC), Boeing (BA), Ford (F), and Eli Lilly (LLY) also open their books.
It's shaping up to be another strong earnings season. According to FactSet data, nearly a quarter of S&P 500 companies have already reported Q3 earnings so far, with an overall earnings growth rate of 29.5%. If that rate holds, it will mark the third straight quarter of earnings growth above 25%.
- Ines Ferré
UPS stock jumps on quarterly results, CEO says 'outlook for holiday demand is strong'
United Parcel Service (UPS) stock rose 2% on Tuesday after the courier posted third quarter results and raised its full-year guidance, signaling solid demand during the upcoming holiday season.
Revenue is expected to come in at $92.6 billion this year, up from a prior forecast of $91.2 billion. UPS also increased its adjusted earnings guidance.
Despite inflation pressures and high diesel costs, UPS is optimistic heading into the last few months of the year.
"US consumers remain resilient and the outlook for holiday demand is strong," CEO Carol Tomé said on the company's earnings call.
The company is in the middle of a multiyear turnaround plan aimed at cost-cutting and reconfiguring its delivery network.
- Grace O'Donnell
JetBlue shares jump on Q3 results and 2027 outlook
Investing.com reports:
JetBlue Airways (JBLU) shares rose more than 14% in premarket trading on Tuesday following the release of third-quarter results and guidance for 2027. The airline reported a loss per share of $0.60, compared to analyst estimates of $0.54. Revenue reached $2.81 billion, slightly below the $2.83 billion consensus estimate.
The airline posted an operating margin of negative 5.1% for the quarter. Operating revenue totaled $2.81 billion while operating expenses came in at $2.96 billion. The company's operating revenue increased 21% year-over-year.
Chief Executive Officer Joanna Geraghty said resilient demand and strong yields drove revenue ahead of initial expectations, allowing the company to offset more of the fuel cost increases than anticipated. She noted that Fort Lauderdale continues to deliver strong results even as the company grows capacity in that market.
- Grace O'Donnell
Coca-Cola raises earnings outlook as North America business slows
Yahoo Finance's Brooke DiPalma reports:
Coca-Cola (KO) posted better-than-expected third quarter results and raised its earnings outlook, but the company saw slowing demand in its North American business.
Coca-Cola stock traded lower in early trading.
The company posted adjusted earnings of $0.91 per share, above the $0.88 expected by Wall Street analysts, alongside revenue of $13.4 billion, also higher than estimates of $12.9 billion.
Overall unit case volume grew by 5%, more than the roughly 3% expected. The increase was once again led by Coke Zero, which grew roughly 16% year over year. Diet Coke and Coca-Cola Light grew by 6%.
- Grace O'Donnell
